{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nv-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"49ea851aef59b9629af8217f764ac0e39a398019c13b9b569f6a3898e9552a74","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:10","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","source_liveness_sha256":"0dfbf3aa4b4798b88d69252e076642b5f0a38751c5010711fbce93c8a7d6e292"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Seat belts, child restraints and unattended children and pets","heading":"C — Buckle up: Nevada seat belt equipment and use rules, child restraint ages and heights, rear-facing infants, airbag dangers, and leaving children or pets in a vehicle","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Buckle up: Nevada seat belt equipment and use rules, child restraint ages and heights, rear-facing infants, airbag dangers, and leaving children or pets in a vehicle
Knowledge domain: who must wear a belt in Nevada, which model years must have which belts, when a child needs an approved restraint or a rear-facing seat in the back, why infants never ride in front of an airbag, and the misdemeanor rules on leaving young children, dogs or cats in a vehicle.

FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A01
Nevada calls seat belts your best protection against injury or death in a crash, and wearing them is required by law, not just advised. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A01
In 2020, drivers who were not wearing seat belts made up 23.03% of Nevada highway fatalities, an increase of 1.15% over 2016. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A01
From 2016 to 2020, 345 unbelted vehicle occupants were killed in Nevada. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A01
A car of model year 1968 or newer must have lap-type seat belts for the front-seat passengers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A01
A car of model year 1970 or newer must have lap-type belts for every passenger plus shoulder harnesses for the front seat. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A01
The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle has one. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A01
Children under six, and children shorter than 57 inches, must ride in an approved child restraint system (NRS 484B.157). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A01
Failing to restrain a child under six or under 57 inches can lead to fines, community service, a license suspension, or a combination of these. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A01
A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child restraint system in the back seat. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A01
Never hold a child on your lap or share one safety belt between a child and another person. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A01
Do not leave a child aged 7 or younger alone in a vehicle when conditions pose a significant risk to the child's health and safety, unless a person at least 12 years old is supervising within sight (NRS 202.485). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A01
Leaving a dog or cat unattended in a vehicle during extreme heat or cold is illegal, and police officers, firefighters and other officials are allowed to use reasonable force to free the animal (NRS 202.487). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A01
Breaking the unattended-child or unattended-pet law is a misdemeanor. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A02
Booster seats and belt-positioning seats raise or position a child so the vehicle's seat belt can secure the child safely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A02
Before travelling with a child, check that the restraint is approved by the US Department of Transportation under the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and suits the child's size and weight. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A02
A child restraint must be installed safely and securely, following the manufacturer's instructions or another method approved by NHTSA. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A02
Infants are always buckled in facing the rear, because a rear-facing seat supports the baby's head and shields the neck and spine in most crashes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A02
The back seat is generally the safest place for children; an older child who must ride in front should have the vehicle seat moved as far back as it goes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A02
To keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag, use a restraint with a full harness or a properly fitted shoulder and lap belt. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A02
Passengers who are unbuckled or sitting too close to an airbag can be badly hurt even in a minor collision or a sudden stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A02
Never place an infant in the front seat of a car that has a passenger-side airbag, because the airbag bursts out of the dashboard at 200 mph and can strike the back of the baby's head through the safety seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

Misconceptions: the belt law covers passengers too, not only the driver; age six alone does not end the child-restraint rule, a child under fifty-seven inches still needs a restraint; a rear-facing seat in the front passenger seat is not safe when that seat has an airbag; leaving a pet in a hot or freezing car is a crime, not just poor judgment.
Mnemonics: under two, rear-facing in back; under six or under fifty-seven inches, approved restraint; seven or younger never left alone without a watcher of twelve or more.
Glossary: child restraint system means an approved car seat, booster or belt-positioning seat; rear-facing seat means a seat installed so the baby faces the back of the car; shoulder harness means the upper-body belt paired with the lap belt; belt-positioning seat means a booster that routes the adult belt correctly over a child.
Dynamic facts: the crash-fatality statistics cite a fixed reporting period and will be replaced in later editions; they are context, not rules to memorize.
